fields.title: Outcomes and Significance - Mission Quiz
fields.description: Five questions covering the same topics on every attempt. Pass with at least three correct.

fields.title: Ask What Changed
fields.content:
An aim is what people hope to change. An outcome is what happens. Keep these in separate boxes in your evidence journal. A movement can oppose a policy without removing that policy everywhere. A record of protest tells us that people acted; it does not by itself prove that every demand was achieved.

Use the early revolts from this chapter as case studies. First name the concern, then the action, then a result actually supported by a source. If the result is not supplied, mark it as a question to investigate. Do not fill the empty box with a victory or defeat you have guessed. People and communities mattered even when their aims were not fully reached. Explaining an outcome carefully is different from giving people a score for winning a battle.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain when you need help, then try your decision again.

fields.title: A Long Movement Has Several Stages
fields.content:
The movement associated with Francisco Dagohoy in Bohol lasted from 1744 to 1829. CulturEd describes communities and local governments linked to the movement. This is evidence of sustained organization. A movement lasting many years can have changing leaders, circumstances and results. Its length is useful evidence, but it is not the same as a list of every aim achieved.

The same account says the movement continued after Dagohoy and that his date of death is uncertain. Do not treat the movement dates as his lifespan or say he personally led every year. Ask a smaller, clearer question: Did organization continue? That is different from asking whether colonial rule ended throughout the Philippines. Keep the place, period and kind of achievement in your explanation. One word such as successful needs a clear meaning and supporting evidence.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain when you need help, then try your decision again.

fields.title: Ask About People Afterward
fields.content:
A report about a leader does not tell the whole story of a community. After resistance, families and participants might have different experiences. To investigate effects, look for records about the people, place and time you are describing. Do not invent the fate of an unnamed household from the fate of a leader. An honest answer can identify what is known and what still needs evidence.

Compare two teaching cards: one records a change of leadership and the other asks what happened to local households. These are different questions. A leadership change can be established by a biography, while a household question needs evidence about those households. A missing account does not mean that people felt nothing or that everyone had the same experience. Studying outcomes includes asking about ordinary people, with respect for the limits of surviving records. These cards are modern learning tools, not historical household records.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain when you need help, then try your decision again.

fields.title: An Event and Its Later Remembrance
fields.content:
The National Museum describes paintings of the Basi Revolt of 1807. The paintings were made in 1821, after the event. They later received recognition as National Cultural Treasure in 2009. Put these on three separate timeline cards: event, representation and later recognition. They answer different historical questions.

A later painting can help us study how an event was represented. It is not a photograph made during the revolt. Museum recognition tells us about later cultural value; it does not tell us that the participants won every demand in 1807. When you use an image, ask when it was made and what kind of source it is. Our diagram is a modern teaching timeline, not one of the historical paintings. You can value a work of art while still checking the evidence for an event. Do not mix up the date of an event with the date of its remembrance.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain when you need help, then try your decision again.

fields.title: Explain Why a Revolt Matters
fields.content:
Early resistance helps us investigate concerns about colonial policies, authority, belief and local life. Comparing cases shows differences in place, time, action and participation. A movement can matter to history even when a particular aim was not achieved. Its significance needs an explanation connected to evidence, rather than a label such as winner or loser.

Build a short museum label: name the case, state one supported result, and explain what it helps us understand. Keep later remembrance separate. Do not claim that all early revolts shared one national plan or that a later event was certain to happen. Similar concerns do not prove that separate movements worked together. Later chapters will examine changing ideas with their own evidence. Your job now is to make a fair explanation of early resistance, including differences and unanswered questions. This is historical investigation, not a contest about which community was best.

Open the three clues. Choose the explanation supported by the evidence. Use Explain when you need help, then try your decision again.

fields.title: Your Outcomes Evidence Journal
fields.content:
Review your journal before the mission quiz. Sort each note into an aim, action, supported result or later remembrance. These categories help you explain what happened without pretending that all movements had the same experience.

The movement associated with Francisco Dagohoy in Bohol lasted from 1744 to 1829. CulturEd describes communities and local governments linked to the movement. This is evidence of sustained organization. A movement lasting many years can have changing leaders, circumstances and results. Its length is useful evidence, but it is not the same as a list of every aim achieved.

Build a short museum label: name the case, state one supported result, and explain what it helps us understand. Keep later remembrance separate. Do not claim that all early revolts shared one national plan or that a later event was certain to happen. Similar concerns do not prove that separate movements worked together. Later chapters will examine changing ideas with their own evidence. Your job now is to make a fair explanation of early resistance, including differences and unanswered questions. This is historical investigation, not a contest about which community was best.

Completing this mission does not complete the chapter. The chapter challenge will bring the five missions together once it is available.
